title: Pattern Generation for Micropattern Traction Microscopy
protocol: Create the design for the photomask using AutoCAD or similar software.
Coat one side of the photomask, which is a thin piece of glass, with a thin layer of chrome.
Design the photomask to create a silicone master with the inverse features desired on the final PDMS stamps when UV light shines through it onto the photoresist.
Cure the negative photoresist by exposing it to UV light.
Remove the uncured SU-8 with a chemical solvent.
Design the photomask consisting of two squares, each measuring 1.5 x 1.5 cm.
Create an even grid of 2 µm circles spaced 6 µm center-to-center on one square.
Form islands with grids of 2 µm circles in another square, varying sizes to include 6 x 6 dots, 12 x 12 dots, 25 x 25 dots, and 42 x 42 dots.
Coat the chosen silicon wafer evenly with photoresist within a cleanroom environment.
Optionally surface-treat the wafer in a plasma asher before applying photoresist coating to enhance SU-8 binding and prevent delamination.
Spin the coated wafer according to manufacturer’s instructions for creating desired feature thickness, adjusting spin time based on resist type and required thickness.
Coat the wafer with photoresist by spinning at 500 RPM for 10 seconds with a ramp of 100 RPM/s.
Reduce the resist thickness to roughly 5 µm by spinning the wafer at 3,000 RPM with a ramp of 300 RPM/s for 30 seconds.
Slowly decelerate the wafer after spinning by reducing the speed to 0 RPM with a ramp of 500 RPM/s for 1 second.
Prepare the resist for UV exposure by baking it briefly on a 95 °C hot plate for 2 minutes.
Expose the resist to UV light using an exposure energy of 105 mJ/cm².
Calculate the exposure time by dividing the exposure energy by the power of the lamp (8 mW), resulting in 13.1 seconds.
Bake the wafer again on a 95 °C hot plate for 3 minutes to set the SU-8 features following development.
Remove uncured SU-8 from the silicon wafer using SU-8 developer.
Mix PDMS in the correct ratio of curing agent to base based on the manufacturer's instructions.
Let the mixture sit at room temperature and pressure for 15 min.
Degas the mixture under vacuum for 15 min.
Pour the PDMS into the master.
Put the assembly into an incubator set to 37 °C overnight to cure.
Remove the master from the incubator.
Allow the cooled master to reach room temperature.
Sonnaicate 25 mm coverslips in ethanol for 10 min.
Thoroughly rinse the sonicated coverslips with deionized (DI) water.
Dry the coverslips using a filtered air gun.
Plasma treat the coverslips for 1 min using a plasma cleaner under vacuum on high (radio frequency power of 30 W).
Release the vacuum slowly after treatment to prevent the coverslips from moving inside the chamber.
Coat each coverslip with 100 µL of fluorescent-labeled protein solution at a concentration of at least 100 µg/mL in a room devoid of direct sunlight/overhead lighting.
Cover for extra protection from light.
Let it sit for 20 min.
Combine unlabeled fibronectin of known concentration and volume with the appropriate amount of AlexaFluor 488 dye in a 1.5 mL tube.
Cover the tube with aluminum foil to protect the dye from light.
Incubate the tube at room temperature for 1 hour, mixing gently every 10 minutes by turning the tube upside down 5-10 times.
Rinse each coverslip thoroughly with DI water.
Remove excess water from the surface of each coverslip by gently tapping the sides onto a paper towel or similarly absorbent material.
Leave the coverslips uncovered in the dark for at least 30 minutes to allow them to dry completely.
Cut the PDMS stamp carefully from the master using a scalpel or other sharp blade.
Plasma treat the PDMS stamps for 2 minutes under vacuum on high (radio frequency power of 30 W).
Within a fume hood, place the stamps in a container with a lid.
Coat each stamp with a very thin layer (<100 µL) of 10% (3-aminopropyl)trimethoxysilane (3-APTMS) diluted in 100% ethanol.
Rinse each stamp on both sides thoroughly with DI water.
Place the stamps in a clean container and coat them liberally with 2.5% glutaraldehyde in DI water.
Cover the stamps and let them sit at room temperature for 30 minutes.
Rinse the stamps thoroughly with DI water.
Remove excess water from the surface of the stamps as done for the coverslips.
Allow the stamps to dry uncovered for approximately 30 minutes.
Check if both protein-coated coverslips and stamps are completely dry.
Use a filtered air gun to ensure complete drying if necessary, avoiding prolonged light exposure for coverslips.
Push the stamps pattern side down onto the coverslips with enough pressure for full contact.
Leave the stamps in contact with the coverslips for 15 minutes.
Carefully peel the PDMS stamps off the coverslips after 15 minutes.
Sonicate 30 mm coverslips in 100% ethanol for 10 min.
Rinse sonicated coverslips with DI water and thoroughly dry with a filtered air gun.
Plasma treat the coverslips for 1 min on high (radio frequency power of 30 W).
Place each plasma-treated coverslip into a well of a 6-well plate.
Coat each coverslip with a very thin layer of 5% APTMS in ethanol in a fume hood.
Cover the 6-well plate and let the coverslips sit for 5 min.
Rinse the coverslips (both sides) and the inside of each well thoroughly with DI water.
Remove excess water inside the wells.
Place the coverslips back in the 6-well plate.
Add approximately 2 mL of 0.5% glutaraldehyde in DI water.
Cover the 6-well plate.
Let the coverslips sit in the glutaraldehyde solution for 30 min.
Thoroughly rinse both the coverslips and the wells of each plate with DI water.
Store the treated coverslips in DI water within the 6-well plates for up to two weeks or use them immediately.
Ensure the coverslips are completely dry before use.
Add 1.25 mL of 40% acrylamide in DI water to a 15 mL conical tube.
Add 175 µL of bis-acrylamide solution in DI water to the same tube.
Add 500 µL of 10x phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) to the tube.
Add 2.915 mL of DI water to the tube.
Pipette 969 μL of this precursor into a 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube.
Store the remaining precursor at 4 °C for up to two weeks.
Measure out ~50-100 mg of ammonium persulfate (APS) in another microcentrifuge tube.
Dilute APS in DI water down to 100 mg/mL.
Set aside the diluted APS for use later.
Open the NHS ester and measure up to 3 mg of NHS in a microcentrifuge tube.
Dilute the NHS-ester to 1 mg/mL in 1x PBS.
Add 2 µL of tetramethylethylenediamine (TEMED) to the microcentrifuge tube containing the 969 µL aliquot of PAA precursor.
Add 15 µL of 1 M hydrochloric acid to decrease the pH of the hydrogel solution.
Add 10 µL of the NHS-ester solution to the tube.
Place the 30 mm coverslip within the metal part of the coverslip dish set with the 3-APTMS and glutaraldehyde-treated side up.
Screw the plastic ring on top of the coverslip dish.
Pipette 5 μL of APS solution into the rest of the PAA precursor in the microcentrifuge tube.
Invert the microcentrifuge tube to mix the contents thoroughly.
Immediately pipette 35 μL of the mixed solution onto a 30 mm coverslip.
Place the patterned coverslip protein side down onto the solution carefully, avoiding air bubbles.
Protect the hydrogel from light and allow it to polymerize for 90 minutes.
Use a razor blade or scalpel to remove the upper coverslip after polymerization, ensuring no sliding or falling back of the coverslip onto the gel.
Add 2 mL of sterile PBS to the gel and incubate at 37 °C for 45 min to passivate any remaining NHS-ester in the hydrogel.
Immediately prepare the gels for experiments or store them overnight in sterile PBS at 4 °C until use.
Turn on the heat (37 °C) and humidity (70%) in the microscope the afternoon before a planned experiment to equilibrate equipment inside the chamber.
Just prior to starting the experiment, turn on the chamber's CO2 source.
Fix the interchangeable coverslip dish set holding the cell-seeded hydrogel to the microscope stage with double-sided tape.
Locate frames of interest for imaging within the gel.
Save each stage position corresponding to sections to be imaged.
Set the microscope software to image each frame in brightfield view once every 5 minutes for 2 hours.
Set the microscope software to image each frame in fluorescent view, corresponding to labeled protein, once every 5 minutes for 2 hours.
In an image processing software, open all individual images taken during a timelapse experiment from each microscope view used in order, from the first to the last image captured.
Turn the opened images into a single image stack by clicking on Image | Stacks | Images to Stack.
Ensure there are two separate image stacks: one of the brightfield view of the cells and one of the fluorescent view of the pattern to which they are attached.

Process the image stack with the StackReg plugin if drifting in the fluorescent images is observed (i.e., the island of interest moves around in the x- and/or y-direction between each frame by >1-2 µm).
Recenter each image in the stack based on the position of the first image using Plugins | StackReg | Translation | OK.
Input the brightfield and fluorescent image stacks into CTFTimelapse.m (Supplemental File 2).
Comment out all but the elastic modulus of the gel being analyzed.
Add the specific elastic modulus value if not present.
Specify dot radius on line 15 (e.g., 1 × 10-6 m).
Specify maximum possible dot diameter on line 16 (e.g., 2.5 µm).
Comment out all but the pixel ratio of the images being analyzed.
Add the specific pixel ratio value if not present.
Specify file directory on lines 35 and 87 for image processing files.
Wait for two figures and one dialogue box to appear.
Use Figure 1 to ensure that the program has found the correct dots.
Use Figure 2 to choose the rectangular grid that helps the program locate and calculate cellular traction forces.
Choose four different dots in Figure 2 to create a rectangular grid around and including the cell/cluster on that pattern.
Select each dot one by one with a left click of the mouse.
Confirm selection by pressing Enter on the button in the dialog box.
Keep count of how many dots are between the first and second dot as well as the first and third dot.
Enter these values into the command window when prompted.
Wait for the script to calculate displacement vectors (u) for each fluorescent dot.
Calculate traction force vectors (F) using Eq (1).
Ensure that the substrate is an infinite elastic half-space and traction forces are applied at the center of each circular dot marker.
Verify that spacing between dot markers is sufficiently large so that their respective displacements do not interact with each other.
Check for inward pointing traction arrows inside the cell/cluster.
Exclude areas outside the cell/cluster from having traction arrows present.
Select an appropriate region of interest (ROI) surrounding the cell/cluster, which includes all traction arrows within the cell using the cursor.
Draw the ROI by left-clicking as many times as necessary to form a polygon shape around the selected area.
Adjust the shape or move the ROI after it is drawn by left-clicking on the corners or edges, respectively.
Double left-click to move on to the next image in the stack once the ROI is drawn correctly.
Repeat this process for all images in the brightfield stack.
